passage:
It was exam week, and the library was packed and hot. Manjula noticed Sangeeta kept a small envelope tucked in her maths book and went quiet every time someone came near.
"What's in it?" Manjula whispered. Sangeeta shook her head.
At lunch Manjula asked again. And again at the water cooler. "Just tell me. I'm your best friend."
Sangeeta's jaw tightened. "Please stop asking."
Manjula stopped. Her curiosity was burning, but Sangeeta looked tired and close to tears.
After the last exam she said, "Sorry for pushing. If you ever want to talk, I'm here. If not, that's okay too."
Sangeeta squeezed her hand. "Thanks. Maybe later."

qa.q: Where did Sangeeta keep the envelope?
qa.a: Tucked in her maths book.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling while she kept asking?
qa.a: She felt intensely curious, as if her curiosity was burning, and a bit left out.

qa.q: What did Manjula do that showed trust?
qa.a: She apologised for pushing, said she was there if Sangeeta wanted to talk, and let it go.

qa.q: How did Manjula's questions feel to Sangeeta?
qa.a: They felt like pressure; Sangeeta's jaw tightened and she asked Manjula to stop.

grounding: A girl keeps asking her friend what she is hiding, sees it invades her space, then says she is there if needed and lets it go.

passage:
In their Mumbai building, Vasudha had started skipping evening cycling. When Nilesh knocked, she said, "Not today," and closed the door quickly.
Nilesh couldn't stand it. "What's going on? Is something wrong? Tell me." He asked in the lift. He asked on the stairs. He even asked her little brother.
On Friday, Vasudha snapped. "Nilesh, stop! Not everything is your business."
Nilesh went red. She was right. He'd been poking and poking.
The next day he left a note under her door: "Sorry for pushing. I'm around whenever you feel like talking. Cycling at five, if you feel like it."
At five, Vasudha came down with her cycle.

qa.q: Where did Nilesh leave his note?
qa.a: Under Vasudha's door.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when Vasudha snapped at him?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, going red, as he realised he had been pushing too much.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that gave Vasudha a choice?
qa.a: He apologised, said he was there if she wanted to talk, and simply invited her to cycling without more questions.

qa.q: How did Nilesh's questions feel to Vasudha?
qa.a: They felt intrusive; she snapped that not everything was his business.

grounding: A boy keeps pressing a friend about what she is hiding, sees it invades her space, then apologises, offers to listen and leaves the choice to her.

passage:
"Kashish, come sit by your Rafiq Nana. When I was ten, the whole class whispered about a girl called Zohra. Her father's shop had closed and her family had moved into one small room.
Everyone wanted details. I did too. It felt like being part of something, knowing the story.
But one day I saw Zohra's face when two boys laughed near her. She looked as if the ground had opened.
So when the whispers started at lunch, I asked about the cricket match instead. When someone told me something new about her, I didn't pass it on.
It sounds small. But I've never forgotten her face."

qa.q: What had happened to Zohra's father's shop?
qa.a: It had closed.

qa.q: Why did young Rafiq want to hear the gossip about Zohra?
qa.a: He felt curious and wanted to belong, as knowing the story felt like being part of the group.

qa.q: What turning point changed how young Rafiq acted?
qa.a: Seeing Zohra's face when boys laughed near her, after which he changed the topic and didn't pass stories on.

qa.q: How might Zohra have felt about the whispering?
qa.a: Zohra felt deeply hurt and exposed, as if the ground had opened under her.

grounding: A grandfather recalls wanting to know gossip about a girl's family trouble, then changing the topic and not passing it on once he saw her pain.

passage:
The school trip bus was stuck at a railway crossing, and everyone was bored. At the back, a group started whispering about Uma. "Her family got thrown out of their flat. They're living with her aunt now."
Preeti leaned in. She wanted to know more. Everyone else did.
Then she glanced forward and saw Uma, alone by the window, earphones in, staring at nothing.
Preeti's stomach turned. The whispers were built on someone's worst month.
"Hey," she said to the group, "who wants to play twenty questions?"
Someone groaned. But two others joined in, and the whispers faded. Preeti didn't repeat what she'd heard to anyone.

qa.q: Where was the bus stuck?
qa.a: At a railway crossing.

qa.q: What did Preeti feel when she saw Uma alone by the window?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and sorry, her stomach turning as she realised the gossip was built on Uma's pain.

qa.q: What did Preeti do instead of joining the gossip?
qa.a: She changed the topic by starting a game and didn't pass on what she had heard.

qa.q: How might Uma feel if she heard the whispers?
qa.a: Uma would likely feel exposed and ashamed about something that wasn't her fault.

grounding: Classmates whisper about a girl's family trouble; the protagonist is curious but, seeing the girl's pain, changes the topic and does not pass it on.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Tuesday.
Last week Ganga laughed at Rashmi's handwriting in front of the class. On Friday, Rashmi told a few girls that Ganga "steals from other people's bags". By Monday, half the class believed it, and one girl moved her bag away from Ganga.
Ganga came to me crying. When I spoke to Rashmi, she admitted it quickly. She looked shocked at how far it had spread. "I only told two people," she said.
I explained that a rumour can't be taken back once it's out. Rashmi apologised to Ganga and helped me correct it with the class. I suggested next time she tell the person directly, or come to me.

qa.q: What did Rashmi say Ganga does?
qa.a: That Ganga steals from other people's bags.

qa.q: How did Rashmi seem to feel when she saw how far the rumour had spread?
qa.a: She seemed shocked and guilty, saying she had only told two people.

qa.q: What could Rashmi have done instead of spreading a rumour?
qa.a: She could have told Ganga directly how the laughing hurt, or asked a teacher for help.

qa.q: How did the rumour affect Ganga?
qa.a: Ganga was hurt and upset; she came to the teacher crying after a classmate moved her bag away.

grounding: A girl spreads a rumour because a classmate was mean to her; it grows out of control, and a teacher shows her rumours cannot be recalled and that telling directly is wiser.

passage:
Thursday
Today in English Irawati called my poem "baby rhymes" and everyone laughed. I was so angry.
So at lunch I told Kunal that Irawati copied the answers in the quiz last week. It felt good for about five minutes.
By sixth period, three different people asked Irawati if she was a cheater. She went bright red and stared at her book.
Now I feel sick. It wasn't even true. I can't pull it back. It's everywhere.
I should have just told her it hurt when she laughed. Tomorrow I'm going to Ma'am and telling her what I did, and I'll say sorry to Irawati.
Siddharth

qa.q: What did Irawati call Siddharth's poem?
qa.a: "Baby rhymes".

qa.q: How does Siddharth feel after seeing Irawati go red?
qa.a: Siddharth feels sick and guilty, knowing the rumour wasn't true and can't be pulled back.

qa.q: What does Siddharth realise would have been better?
qa.a: Telling Irawati directly that her laughing hurt, and now going to the teacher and apologising.

qa.q: How did the rumour affect Irawati?
qa.a: Irawati was embarrassed and hurt, going bright red when people asked if she was a cheater.

grounding: Siddharth spreads a rumour because a classmate was mean; it grows out of control, and Siddharth sees it cannot be recalled and plans to tell the teacher.

passage:
"Pankaj, your Maria Aunty once wanted to disappear. I was eleven. Someone started a story that I had stolen the class teacher's gold pen. By lunch, everyone knew. Girls moved away when I walked by. I felt like I was made of glass.
I hadn't done it. It wasn't my fault. But it felt like it was.
That evening I told my father everything. The next day he came with me to the teacher, who found out the pen had simply fallen behind a cupboard.
I also went to the girl who started it and said, 'Please stop. It isn't true.' And my two real friends sat with me every lunch until it died down."

qa.q: What was young Maria accused of stealing?
qa.a: The class teacher's gold pen.

qa.q: How did young Maria feel when the rumour spread?
qa.a: She felt exposed and ashamed, as if she were made of glass, and wanted to disappear.

qa.q: What choices in the story helped young Maria?
qa.a: Telling her father, who went with her to the teacher, asking the girl who started it to stop, and staying close to her real friends.

qa.q: How might the girl who started the rumour have felt when Maria confronted her?
qa.a: She may have felt caught out and embarrassed, especially once the pen was found.

grounding: An aunt recalls a false rumour about her; she felt exposed, told a trusted adult, asked the source to stop and held onto her real friends.

passage:

passage:
"Ganga, let your Lokesh Mama tell you something. When I was twelve, my friends sat under the banyan tree every afternoon, and one day they started on Bhola. He was my friend too. They laughed about his torn chappals and his father's drinking.
I felt sick. I liked Bhola.
I said, 'That's not nice. He's not here to answer.' They rolled their eyes. One called me a spoilsport.
I got up and left. I went to find Bhola at the pond, and we skimmed stones.
It cost me a few afternoons under the banyan tree. But Bhola never forgot it, and neither did I."

qa.q: Where did young Lokesh's friends sit every afternoon?
qa.a: Under the banyan tree.

qa.q: How did young Lokesh feel when his friends gossiped about Bhola?
qa.a: He felt sick and uneasy, because he liked Bhola.

qa.q: What turning point in the story showed loyalty?
qa.a: When young Lokesh said it wasn't nice to talk about someone who wasn't there, then got up and left to be with Bhola.

qa.q: How might the friends under the tree have seen Lokesh?
qa.a: They saw him as a spoilsport, rolling their eyes at him.

grounding: An uncle recalls friends gossiping about someone he liked; he said it was not nice, refused to join, and left.

Giggles rippled across the room.
Disha's chest tightened. She liked Sarita. Sarita shared her tamarind sweets and helped her with Hindi.

passage:
I'm Zainab. In Class 6, the girls I sat with loved gossip. One day they started on Chaitanya, the quiet boy who ate lunch alone. "He smells like onions." "He's so weird."
I didn't join in. But I was scared. What would they say about me if I didn't laugh?
So sometimes I laughed a little. And every time I felt worse.
Then one day I heard them whispering about me after I left the table. That was when I understood: a group that needs cruelty isn't safe for anyone.
I stayed polite, but I stopped sitting with them. I started eating with the chess club kids. Chaitanya was one of them.

qa.q: What did the girls say Chaitanya smelled like?
qa.a: Onions.

qa.q: What was Zainab afraid of?
qa.a: Zainab feared that without laughing along, Zainab would become the group's next target.

qa.q: What did Zainab do once the fear came true?
qa.a: Zainab stayed polite but stopped sitting with the gossiping group and found kinder friends at the chess club.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt eating lunch alone?
qa.a: Chaitanya may have felt lonely and left out, especially if he sensed people talking about him.

grounding: Zainab fears being gossiped about if not joining in, sees a group that needs cruelty is not safe, and moves to kinder friends.

passage:
In their Kraków school, Marek heard from a friend that Valentina had cheated on the geography test. He repeated it to two boys at lunch without thinking.
By afternoon, it was everywhere. Valentina sat in the corridor crying into her sleeve.
Then Marek heard from the teacher that Valentina's paper had been checked twice. She hadn't cheated at all.
Marek felt awful. His stomach dropped through the floor.
He went to her. "Valentina, I'm really sorry. I repeated it and it wasn't true." Then he went back to the two boys. "What I said about Valentina was wrong. She didn't cheat."
Valentina wiped her eyes. "Thanks for fixing it."

qa.q: Which test was Valentina said to have cheated on?
qa.a: The geography test.

qa.q: How did Marek feel when he learned the truth?
qa.a: He felt awful and guilty, his stomach dropping through the floor.

qa.q: What did Marek do to repair the harm?
qa.a: He apologised to Valentina and went back to the boys he told to correct the rumour.

qa.q: How might Valentina feel when Marek corrects the story?
qa.a: Valentina felt relieved and thankful that he was fixing it.

grounding: A boy repeats something false and a girl cries; he feels awful, apologises and corrects the rumour, using guilt to become kinder.

passage:

A few girls turned to Irawati, eager for her reaction.
Irawati imagined standing where Hafsa was, three people behind, hearing her family talked about just before an exam. Her stomach clenched.

passage:
At the Lucknow school canteen, Avni's friends were laughing about Rehana's new haircut. "She looks like a boy now." "Maybe her mum cut it with kitchen scissors."
Avni looked across the canteen. Rehana was sitting alone, touching the back of her head.
Avni remembered when her own hair had been cut too short, and how she'd worn a cap for a week.
"What if it were you they were talking about?" she said. "How would you feel?"
Her friends shifted uncomfortably.
"Anyway, is anyone going to the science fair?" Avni asked. The conversation moved on. Later, she told Rehana, "Your hair looks nice."

qa.q: What were Avni's friends laughing about?

qa.q: What did Avni feel when she saw Rehana touching her hair?
qa.a: She felt empathy, remembering her own too-short haircut and wearing a cap for a week.

qa.a: She asked her friends how they would feel if it were them, then changed the subject to the science fair.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel when Avni compliments her hair?
qa.a: Rehana would likely feel comforted and less self-conscious.

grounding: A girl imagines how it feels to be the one talked about, asks her friends what if it were about them, and changes the subject.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, Friday.
Uma has been spending a lot of time with Ankita this term. I've noticed Ankita tells Uma stories about other girls: who fought with her parents on the phone, who failed her test. Then she asks Uma to share things in return.
Uma came to me today. "I told Ankita that my brother's in hospital. Now half the floor knows."
She looked hurt and wary. She said she'd noticed Ankita seems to enjoy knowing things about everyone.
I told her it's wise to share less with someone like that. Friendship shouldn't feel like a trade. Uma nodded and said she'd be more careful.

qa.q: What did Uma tell Ankita about her brother?
qa.a: That he's in hospital.

qa.q: How did Uma seem to feel when she came to the warden?
qa.a: She seemed hurt and wary, after her private news spread across the floor.

qa.q: What did Uma decide to do?
qa.a: She decided to share less with Ankita and be more careful.

qa.q: How might Ankita see the information she collects?
qa.a: Ankita seems to use information to feel powerful and important.

grounding: A friend passes on stories about others and asks for secrets in return; the girl notices it is used for power and decides to share less.

passage:
Tuesday
Anjali always has news. Who cried in the washroom. Whose parents shouted at the PTM. Today she told me three things about three different people before lunch.
Then she said, "Your turn. Tell me something about your sister."
I felt weird. Like it was a shop, and I had to pay.
I said, "There's nothing to tell."
She looked annoyed. "You're no fun."
I've noticed that everything I tell her gets around. And she seems to like knowing things that make others look bad.
I'm going to share less with her from now on. Friendship shouldn't feel like trading.

passage:
"Sangeeta, please stay after class."
Her stomach dropped. Joseph Sir waited until the room was empty.
"I've heard that you told people Rohan cheated on the maths quiz. Is that true?"
Sangeeta wanted to say no. She wanted to say someone else started it.
"Sangeeta?"
She took a breath. "Yes, Sir. I said it. I was angry because he got a better mark."
"Thank you for being honest. That was hard."
"Am I in trouble?"
"There'll be consequences. You'll apologise to Rohan and help me set the record straight with the class. But lying would have made it much worse."
Sangeeta nodded. "I'm sorry."

qa.q: What did Sangeeta tell people about Rohan?
qa.a: That he cheated on the maths quiz.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when Joseph Sir asked her to stay?
qa.a: She felt scared, her stomach dropping.

qa.q: Why was Sangeeta's honest answer better than lying?
qa.a: It meant she could apologise and help fix it, while lying would have made things much worse.

qa.q: How might Joseph Sir see Sangeeta's honesty?
qa.a: Joseph Sir respects it, thanking her and saying it was hard to do.

grounding: A teacher calls a girl about a rumour; she is scared but admits it and apologises, accepting consequences instead of lying.

passage:
I'm Vikas. In Class 5, I told everyone that a boy called Ronit had been caught stealing from the canteen. I made it up because he laughed at my football.
The next day, Ayesha Ma'am called me to the staffroom. My hands were shaking.
She asked, "Did you start this story about Ronit?"

"Yes, Ma'am. I made it up. I'm sorry."
She nodded. "Thank you for telling me the truth." I had to apologise to Ronit in front of the class and miss football practice for a week. It hurt. But I think lying would have hurt more.

qa.a: Vikas felt scared, with shaking hands.
